title: The Continuity of Knowledge and the Eternal Light
english: They desire this long life, because they consider no other good than such a state. Just as life now is praiseworthy and forthcoming, so also 'length of days' for this age, so that each doctrine of truth may be known and illuminating, having great light. A praiseworthy day is each practical virtue being made straight.

Since, therefore, just as perfect and complete knowledge will receive here the partial knowledge, so also regarding practical virtue, those who have been proven righteous through practical virtue from there—for they have righteousness now and forthcoming—will be differently eager for 'length of days' for this age, not this common one, but the one capable of having come into being, about which they say: 'This is the day which the Lord has made' (Ps 118:24); for they are pointing to it. But no one points to the future, but to that which is already present and has established itself. The future, when that time comes through which it comes, is no longer future. Again, that too will fall under pointing.

Thus, if you take the king, and even the holy man, and even him who has come forth from Mary, they do not pray about that life or length of perceivable days, but about those already spoken of. They receive long-age life and offer thanks concerning this. And the long-age life is not the life of one age. Appropriately, each age receives life, sometimes as beginning and introductory, sometimes as intermediate, and sometimes as complete.

But after all these spoken days—each doctrine illuminating the soul, being shone upon by the sun of righteousness (Mal 4:2), we have called a day. After these, there is a certain complete state of light in the flashes of progress. That day is not interrupted by night, nor does it become a multitude of days. And it is possible to receive it thus; since the virtues have affinity with one another—for each is luminous—one length of days...

It happens from their following, and it is not interrupted. I say: each scientific principle is separated from the others; for the scientist knows many things. For example, as if it were in medicine, a surgical principle or a dietary one; as if it were in grammar, this or that. When someone is perfected, he no longer possesses these different things; for now it is perhaps more possible to possess the surgical, and less the dietary. But when he presents to me a perfect physician having all the principles perfectly and without excess, they are no longer poured out [distinctly], nor do they have difference even in matter.

Suppose for me a man having complete health according to the body. He no longer needs diet alone, nor incision. He has cast away those things for the sake of which he needed these, and instead he has health that no longer produces anything else. And for his sake all these things are labored for. And the maintenance of it is labored for with a certain desire; for they are just as if they were producing health, so also things protective, such as the gymnasium or such food.

That long day, therefore, is uninterrupted; for it will be a long time before that time is fulfilled: 'The Lord will be to you an eternal light' (Isa 60:19), when the sun no longer fails, 'nor shall the rising of the moon light the night' (Rev 21:23). And these things are not said about the sensible luminaries; for 'immediately' 'after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light' (Matt 24:29). But these lights will no longer give [light] to those who are friends of this [world]; for the sun will be sevenfold and the moon like the sun. Generally, it is said concerning the heavens that 'they shall be changed.' And when he says heavens being changed, and the stars and luminaries in them, just as, if we speak concerning the earth: 'all the earth worships,' we say those dwelling in the earth. 'Sing to the Lord, all the earth' (Ps 96:1). 'Great is your glory in your salvation.' If we receive the glory truly, we do not call the most pleasant state glory. For example, we do not call a human beginning glory, nor a dignity; for all these things are...
